passage: Every morning Harsha took the 9:05 bus from Hassan to the bank branch in Holenarasipur. Gargi from the loans desk had asked twice if he'd join the Sunday cycling group to the lake. Twice he'd said, 'Next week.' Tonight he reached level 400. He felt nothing at all. He put the phone down and stared at the ceiling.

One Monday she took half a day off, caught the bus into town and sat in the clinic waiting room with a token in her hand. Library on Saturday. Doctor on Monday. Both, she decided.

So she changed the pattern on purpose. She swapped her lunchtime scrolling for a walk to the community garden two streets from the office, where an old man named Sipho grew spinach in tyres. He handed her a trowel on the second day. On Saturdays she started a beginners' woodwork class with her friend Omar, who made a spectacularly crooked stool. Some evenings still went grey. She made herself a promise and wrote it on the fridge: If the grey gets heavier or doesn't lift, book the clinic, don't wait. For now, there was spinach to water.

passage: The residential school in the district town was only forty kilometres from Ramesh's village, but at night it felt like the other side of the world. Lying on the top bunk, he listened for sounds that weren't there: the cow shifting in the shed, Bou's bangles as she scrubbed the vessels, the dog barking at the moon. Instead there were twenty boys breathing and a tap dripping. He thought of the cold rice and curd Bou gave him on summer afternoons, and his throat went tight. Below him, Pintu snored. Ramesh pressed his face into the pillow so nobody would hear. Fourteen was too old to miss your mother. Everyone said so. In the morning, Yamini Didi, the matron, noticed his swollen eyes at the tap and quietly asked him to help her count the laundry.

At breakfast, his friend Yara said, 'I miss my little brothers so much it hurts.' Abebe laughed and said, 'I don't miss anything. Freedom!' His roommates laughed too. Later, in the library, he opened a photo of the family coffee ceremony and stared at it until the bell rang.
